items.content:
society has solved “collaborating at scale over long horizons with auditability” a few times and it’s often around an immutable log:

•  software / open source: git commit history
•  financial systems / accounting: transaction journals / double-entry ledgers
•  medicine / pharma: EHR audit trails + clinical-trial audit logs
•  aviation — flight data recorders (FDR/CVR) + sequential maintenance event logs
•  nuclear / critical infrastructure — plant operational event logs / SCADA historians
•  scientific research (code & data subsets) — versioned repositories + electronic lab-notebook audit trails

items.content:
This part is spot on: 
> "Overall, we found that we were over-constraining Claude Code...while these constraints were once needed to avoid worst case scenarios, we have since found we can delete many of them and let the model use surrounding context and judgement instead." 

I have a tendency to write extensive prompts that cover every edge case. In the past few months I have come to increasingly come to find that this can lead to counterproductive behavior where the model addresses my specific requests, but doesn't independently provide a new perspective on the problem (explore the "unknown unknowns") 

The model still needs access to your complete context in order to be able to make complete decisions - it just doesn't necessarily need constraints on how to best use that context. Over time I predict we will increasingly defer to the models to help solve these unknown unknowns. 

FWIW I've found Opus 5 to be a fantastic model and continue to consume it heavily through Claude Code

items.content:
AI skills are no longer moving in one straight line.

The market is starting to separate people who only use tools from those who can turn AI into business value.

The data suggests a useful shift: AI capability is a set of different professional paths. 

Microblog by @antgrasso

Deep learning still shows strong demand, which means the foundations of machine learning remain important for many organizations.

At the same time, GenAI is moving into daily operations.

Roles linked to LLMs and agentic AI show that companies are no longer only experimenting with models.

They are trying to connect them to workflows, products, and business processes.

Specialized depth can still carry a premium.

LLM fine-tuning has fewer listings, but the salary signal is strong because this kind of expertise helps organizations adapt models to specific needs rather than relying only on generic tools.

Business judgment is also gaining clear economic value.

AI product management shows that companies need people who can translate technical possibilities into useful products and trusted outcomes.

In my view, the message is practical: learning AI is not just about keeping up with new tools.

The stronger path is to understand where the technology creates value and how it can be governed in real business contexts.

items.title: Text encoders still mostly follow BERT’s basic design, but they are usually evaluated after fine-tun...
items.content:
Text encoders still mostly follow BERT’s basic design, but they are usually evaluated after fine-tuning on a specific task, which makes it difficult to tell whether pretraining itself produced useful representations or whether finetuning repaired them.

In this paper from @AIatMeta and @nyuniversity, the authors separate these effects by keeping the encoder’s weights fixed and training only a small model on top of its outputs. Under this test, larger BERT models become worse at producing representations that can be reused directly, even as they improve at predicting masked words.

CrossBERT changes the architecture so that the main encoder only builds representations, while a smaller predictor reads those representations and reconstructs the missing words.

Across models of several sizes, CrossBERT’s frozen representations improve steadily, while standard BERT’s often decline; it also trains about 1.5–2 times faster and uses training data more efficiently. The experiments offer a clear way to judge what an encoder learned before finetuning and show that a small architectural change can improve both representation quality and training efficiency.

items.content:
The innateness of personality is obvious in kids because they haven't yet had the time to undergo any meaningful environment-induced (or self-induced) change. They express their raw nature.

The person you were born as doesn't have to be the person you die as.

items.content:
@AnthropicAI just released Claude Opus 5. @GoogleDeepMind also released Gemini 3.5 Flash few days back.

Every new model launch creates the same problem for engineering teams:

Do you trust the public benchmarks, build a full internal benchmark, or ignore the release until someone else tests it?

A better first step is much smaller.

We compared Gemini 3.5 Flash with 3.6 Flash on one narrow production-style task: summarizing technical papers under a fixed 180-word limit.

That small set was not enough to approve a migration.

It was enough to reveal what mattered:
> 3.6 retained more required facts
> 3.5 followed the length constraint more reliably
> Both repeatedly lost the same critical qualification

That is the point of a smoke test.

Before spending days building a full benchmark for Opus 5, Gemini 3.5, or the next model release, run 5–10 cases built around failures that would make the model unusable in your system.

The full article walks through how to reuse production failures, build answer cards, grade outputs,  and decide whether a model deserves more evaluation time.

Public benchmarks put a model on your shortlist.

Your own smoke test decides whether it stays there.

AuroraGPT - Built by Scars of Frontline

The theory is nothing. AuroraGPT advances scientific discovery by building generalizable, foundation-scale large-language models across multiple scientific domains, including physics, chemistry, mathematics, and material sciences. In a world dominated by theoretical models and theoritic ideals, AuroraGPT was never born from theoretical laboratory conditions. AuroraGPT forged its foundation in the real-world challenges of exascale computing. Traditional machine learning models operate in narrowly defined, well-structured environments. However, AuroraGPT goes beyond static datasets into domains where mathematics, programming, and extreme complexity dominate. Its architecture generalizes across scientific disciplines, enabling adaptation to evolving scientific data. It also enables faster, scalable, predictive modeling that can adapt to changing scientific data — something conventional models struggle to accomplish at meaningful resolution or exascale computing.

Achieving these objectives required AuroraGPT to survive in the harshest computational environments ever encountered—the early volatile stages of the Aurora Supercomputer. Building at exascale demanded fault-tolerant training algorithms capable of surviving node dropouts, managing inconsistent interconnect bandwidths, and recovering from partial model convergence failures. AuroraGPT’s foundation large language model scaling strategy involved distributing training across 60,000 GPUs while dynamically re-optimizing tensor parallelism, complex mathematics, data parallelism, and pipeline parallelism in fluctuating infrastructure stability. AuroraGPT engineered its resilience mechanisms in direct response to real-world node failures, memory bottlenecks, and system fragmentation — scars from computational battles that ultimately forged a new class of singularity-resilient AI infrastructure.

items.content:
One thing I recommend after you do your blood work is to try fix blood levels with food first

People jump to supplements immediately but I have a lingering and sneaking suspicion that many supplements are literally just markers, as in they're the result of what you do and consume like sun exposure and good food etc

As in you can take Vitamin D pills and your Vitamin D level in your blood will be correct but it may not improve the actual reason why Vitamin D was low (which is lack of sun)

So taking the supplements will bring the markers to proper levels but possibly in 10-20 years we learn that it didn't actually fix the root cause of the markers, just the markers themselves!

This is the type of application I've already built earlier at the beginning of this year for a conference demonstration! 

GPT Paper-Reader, to show how you can leverage the summarization capabilities of large language models to retrieve research papers from databases, summarize their content, and engage in Q&A interactions with people.    The future is here.  In addition to the regular theoretical presentation, I'll be presenting a practical GPT. This application utilizes GPT, to effectively read and analyze complete academic papers:  Basically the app chunks the PDF paper into manageable sections for detailed reading and generates concise summaries for each segment. By maintaining context from previous sections within the token limit, it enhances comprehension. Before diving into the paper, you can outline specific questions in the prompt. This approach allows GPT to extract the most important information during its reading and summarizing process, leading to superior outcomes.   After summarizing all parts, you will receive comprehensive answers to your inquiries based on the consolidated summaries. By default, the initialized prompt will target essential points such as:  These inquiries are tailored for research articles within the computer science domain. Upon completion of the paper review, feel free to engage with the question() interface to ask further questions.
